# Prescriptive lessons -- van-eps x harmonic-mechanisms-vol-1

## maj7

Van Eps treats maj7 not as a four-note block but as a minor triad wearing a major-seventh label: the structural content of any maj7 voicing is one of the pure minor triads embedded within it. This is the single lesson extracted for this quality, and it connects directly to the book's macro-doctrine (Chapter 13) that "major makes minor, and minor makes major" -- seventh chords are triad-over-bass constructions, never independent four-note grips.

- [ch.13 p.276] A maj7 chord **must** contain the notes of one of the three pure minor triads (open or closed). Locate the embedded minor triad first; that triad is the voicing's core, and the remaining tone is the bass or color note. Do not approach maj7 as a freestanding four-note shape.

---

## major-triad

Van Eps builds every major-triad lesson around two load-bearing claims: (1) triads are frozen voice motion, so every grip must be understood as the residue of lines that could move, and (2) the three inversions are the primary organizational universe -- not chord names, not scale-degree functions. The body of prescriptions divides into generative techniques (sixth-deletion, implied tones, delayed coupling, super/sub voice movement, cycle-of-fifths key order, blockout cycling) and hard constraints on physical execution (fatigue-factor fretting economy, no pre-placed fingers, no ringing-over between stations, no four-voice simultaneous sound in double-stop lines, no wrong notes).

- [ch.1 p.11] Internalize every triad inversion as **frozen voice motion**, not a static grip. "Arpeggios are broken chords -- chords are frozen arpeggios." The student's job is to hear the lines that produced the grip.
- [ch.1 p.17] Give inner voices room to sound. Moving lines inside a major-triad texture are masked if the outer voices are too dense; manage voicing register so the inner line can be heard independently.
- [ch.1 p.8] *(proscriptive)* Fret only the strings that are sounding. Extra pressure on muted strings accumulates fatigue and degrades multi-voice control.
- [ch.2 p.18] Transpose all inversion drills through the **descending cycle of fifths** (up a fourth or down a fifth), not chromatically. This is the master organizational order for the entire volume; chromatic key shifts are never the default.
- [ch.2 p.19] For first-inversion major triads, the outer sixth is strong enough to carry the harmonic identity alone: **delete the middle voice** without spoiling the chordal result. The two-note sixth frame is the voicing.
- [ch.2 p.20] Imply tones the hand cannot grip. A note inferred from surrounding voices and overtones is "almost heard" and counts as harmonically real; use this to reduce voicing density while preserving identity.
- [ch.2 p.21] When more notes exist than can be sounded simultaneously, **arpeggiate with delayed coupling**: the ear remembers the first notes and compounds them with the next, forming a unified harmonic picture.
- [ch.2 p.23] Track tonic position as the primary inversion identifier: tonic on top = 1st inversion; tonic second = 2nd inversion; tonic lowest = root position. This is the organizational principle, not the interval stack.
- [ch.5 p.115] *(proscriptive)* Notes within each station must **not ring over** each other unless a tie is written. The harp-like bleed is explicitly rejected; clean station separation is required.
- [ch.5 p.115] When working with sixth intervals derived from first-inversion major triads, **always identify the parent inversion**. Every sixth double-stop is a first- or second-inversion triad with the middle deleted, not a freestanding interval.
- [ch.5 p.115] A first-inversion triad is harmonically present even when the middle voice is absent. Treat the inferred tone as real: "a first inversion triad is inferred with the middle note deleted in the first half of each station."
- [ch.6 p.133] *(proscriptive)* Do not pre-place fingers before the attack in articulated triad passages. Left- and right-hand attack must be simultaneous; anticipatory fretting destroys voice-separation clarity.
- [ch.8 p.160] The super/sub system prescribes raising or lowering any single voice of a major triad by one diatonic step. Raising the middle voice of a first-inversion triad automatically produces a second-inversion member of the family.
- [ch.8 p.160] Keep the **named inversion mentally active** at all times during super/sub work. The named inversion is the origin; losing it causes harmonic disorientation across the voice-motion sequence.
- [ch.8 p.161] Treat every triad inversion as a generative center: moving any voice one step up or down in any scale produces a **new harmonic center**, not merely an embellishment of the original.
- [ch.8 p.163] *(proscriptive)* Accept no wrong notes in super/sub inversion drilling. "Every wrong note plants the germ of a bad habit because the ear retains the sound of the mistake."
- [ch.9 p.175] First-inversion major triads with upper-voice sub motion are **notated identically** to root-position triads with upper-voice super motion. Exploit this identity to move between inversion families without a position shift.
- [ch.9 p.185] *(proscriptive)* In double-stop moving-line passages, **never let four voices sound simultaneously** unless a written hold-over is intended. The previous note of the moving line must be muted before the next is sounded; only three voices should be audible at any moment.
- [ch.10 p.239] Include all root-position voicings regardless of reach difficulty. "These voicings must be included no matter how impractical they may appear, because by design they belong to the family of basic triads."
- [ch.10 p.239] When full sustain is impossible, **compromise fingerings** are acceptable only when the moving voice is detached and sounded separately -- at that point there is no notational difference between original and compromise.
- [ch.11 p.249] Sustain the half note full value when two voices move over it. Releasing early is permitted only as a last resort: "endeavor to sustain the half note full value."
- [ch.13 p.269] Actively seek **nontraditional configurations**. Traditional shapes are already known; unconventional inversion placements and string sets must be found, analyzed, and practiced systematically.
- [ch.13 p.273] Treat the bass as a **fourth independent voice**, entirely separate from the triad. A major triad placed over an unrelated bass is a legitimate four-voice harmonic unit; the bass neither confirms nor contradicts the triad's identity.
- [ch.13 p.277] A cycle-of-fifths bass line is **harmonically neutral** -- neither major nor minor -- until triads are added. The student placing major triad inversions over it is making the quality determination unilaterally.
- [ch.14 p.288] Accept harmonic clashes in blockout studies as productive, not errors. "These dissonances are very helpful and necessary at times." Do not resolve or sidestep them; they are the point of the exercise.
- [ch.14 p.290] In blockout studies, cycle all three major triad inversions in a **fixed repeat order** over an independent chromatic bass. This repeat-order constraint systematizes voice-leading across the descending cycle of fifths.
- [ch.14 p.293] Group certain key cycles by **major thirds** (e.g., C--Ab--E) for concentrated inversion study. These three keys share fingerboard geography and should be studied as a unit before integrating back into the full cycle.

## minor-triad

Van Eps treats minor triads as a fully parallel system to major triads -- same three inversions, same super/sub drilling, same bass-as-independent-fourth-voice doctrine, same cycle-of-fifths transposition order -- but issues two specific warnings against borrowing from the major system: the minor third interval is one semitone shorter than the major third, so shapes do not transfer, and mixed-minor studies (melodic minor ascending, harmonic minor descending) assign different scales to different voices within the same passage. The fatigue-factor and nontraditional-configuration prescriptions apply without modification.

- [ch.3 p.66] When voicing minor triads through inversions in mixed-minor context, assign **melodic minor ascending to the upper moving voice** and **harmonic minor descending to the lower moving voice**. These are not interchangeable; each voice has its own scale source.
- [ch.7 p.159] Minor mode inversion patterns **cannot be mapped from major shapes**. The minor third is one semitone shorter; independent study of minor triad inversions is mandatory.
- [ch.11 p.253] Apply super and sub voice movements to minor triads in both melodic and harmonic minor, in all three inversions, with voice-motion reversal (open to closed). Minor triads get the full super/sub treatment -- no shortcuts.
- [ch.13 p.273] The bass is a **fourth independent voice** beneath minor triads, just as beneath major. A minor triad over an unrelated bass is a legitimate harmonic unit, not an error requiring correction.
- [ch.13 p.269] Seek **nontraditional configurations** for minor triads. Unconventional inversion placements and string sets must be located and practiced; familiar minor shapes are the starting point, not the endpoint.
- [ch.1 p.8] *(proscriptive)* Fret only the strings actually sounding in minor triad voicings. The fatigue-factor rule applies without modification to minor triad inversions, especially those with wide string-set skips.
- [ch.14 p.288] All three minor triad inversions -- root, first, and second -- are employed in blockout studies alongside major inversions. No inversion is optional; all must appear in the repeat-order cycling.

---

## diminished-triad

Van Eps treats the diminished triad as one of four structural exercise types in the chromatic vocabulary, not as a passing or ornamental sonority. A single prescription governs it: the chromatic exercises through all four triad qualities (major, minor, diminished, augmented) are the universal scale-construction source.

- [ch.7 p.149] Drill the diminished triad as one of **four chromatic exercise types** (major, minor, dim, aug). Using these exercises in all their forms, positions, and combinations constructs every major, minor, diminished, and augmented scale. The diminished triad is structural raw material, not a color chord.

---

## augmented-triad

Identical prescription to diminished: the augmented triad is structural chromatic vocabulary, drilled as one of four exercise types for generating the full scale system.

- [ch.7 p.149] Drill the augmented triad as one of **four chromatic exercise types** alongside major, minor, and diminished. The same chromatic exercise system that constructs all scales requires the augmented triad as a constituent; it is a building block, not an ornament.

---

## dom7

Van Eps refuses to assign dominant 7th voicings a fixed identity: the same shape carries multiple harmonic callings depending on its place in a progression, and the most important alternative reading is the enharmonic diminished-ninth. All small chords -- dom7 included -- have second, third, and fourth callings that must be mastered alongside the primary label.

- [ch.7 p.141] A G dominant 7th voicing (degrees 3-5) is simultaneously an **E diminished 9th**. "The symbol for a chord depends on its use -- its place in a progression." Both names must be available to the student for the same fingerboard shape.
- [ch.13 p.276] All small chords, including dom7 configurations, have **multiple harmonic callings** under varied conditions. The primary label is the entry point; fluency requires knowing every harmonic role a given voicing can occupy.

---

## min7

Van Eps derives min7 voicings from embedded major triads via the major-makes-minor identity: the structural content of any min7 is one of the three pure major triads (open or closed). Two lessons cover the same identity from slightly different angles -- one names the minor triad as the content, one states the principle explicitly -- and together they establish that min7 is never a freestanding four-note block.

- [ch.13 p.276] A min7 chord **must contain** the notes of one of the three pure major triads. Locate the embedded major triad first and treat it as the structural core; the remaining tone is bass or color. Do not approach min7 as an independent four-note grip.
- [ch.13 p.276] The gateway to all 7th chord voicing is the **major-makes-minor / minor-makes-major identity**: "major makes minor, and minor makes major." For min7, identify which pure major triad (notes open or closed) supplies the harmonic content, then build outward.

---

## dim7

A single lesson: Van Eps names the diminished 9th as the enharmonic reinterpretation of a dominant 7th voicing, anchoring dim7 thinking to the chameleon-chord doctrine rather than treating it as a standalone quality.

- [ch.7 p.141] A dominant 7th voicing (e.g., G47 degrees 3-5) is simultaneously an **E diminished 9th**. The chord symbol is determined by harmonic context and progression placement, not by the voicing alone. Know both names for every applicable shape.

---

## sixth-chord

Van Eps treats sixth chords entirely as first-inversion triads with the middle voice deleted, not as independent four-note structures. Two prescriptions govern them: the sixth interval is the outer frame of the first-inversion triad, and that frame expands outward to a tenth via upper-voice motion in the 1-5-3-1-5-1-3-5 pulsation pattern.

- [ch.2 p.19] A sixth-chord voicing on guitar is a **first-inversion triad with the middle voice omitted**. "The sixth makes a very powerful two-note chord and because of this power, the middle notes can be deleted without spoiling the chordal result." Do not treat sixth chords as independent four-note grips; derive them from their parent first-inversion triad.
- [ch.5 p.115] The sixth double-stop **opens outward to a tenth** by moving the upper voice up one diatonic step (the 1-5-3-1 upper-line pattern). This is a specific voice-leading move in the sixths-to-tenths studies, not an optional ornament; the expansion must be executed as a deliberate melodic event.
